overview: Pinnacle is an Australia-headquartered, global multi-affiliate investment management firm, founded in 2006 and ASX-listed since 2016. Rather than running its own funds, Pinnacle takes minority or majority equity stakes in a stable of boutique 'Affiliate' investment managers (19 as of FY2026, spanning listed equities, fixed income, private credit, private equity, infrastructure and real assets) and supplies them with distribution, seed/working capital, operations, compliance and responsible-entity services in exchange for a share of their profits. Group FUM has grown from A$19.8bn at FY2016 to A$229.4bn at FY2026 (28% 10-year CAGR), sourced from Australian retail, Australian institutional and increasingly international (33% of FUM) clients.

business_model.summary: Pinnacle earns its own contract revenue (management/distribution/responsible-entity fees charged to Affiliates and funds) plus, more importantly, books its proportional equity-accounted share of each Affiliate's net profit after tax (management fees, performance fees and other affiliate revenue) below the revenue line. Because Affiliate profit share flows in below Pinnacle's own thin revenue line, reported net income is typically 2-4x Pinnacle's own statutory revenue (e.g. FY2026: A$109.7m revenue vs A$176.7m NPAT). Ownership stakes range from ~25% to 100% (fully consolidated where control is achieved, e.g. Pacific Asset Management from April 2026); non-controlled stakes are equity-accounted.

revenue_streams.name: Pinnacle's own contract revenue (distribution/RE/admin fees, dividends from principal investments)
revenue_streams.notes: A$109.7m in FY2026 vs A$65.5m FY2025 (+67%), boosted by PAM consolidation from April 2026

revenue_streams.name: Share of Affiliate net profit after tax (equity-accounted, base management fees)
revenue_streams.notes: A$136.0m in FY2026, +4.9% YoY (understated by PAM's move from equity-accounted to consolidated mid-year)

revenue_streams.name: Share of Affiliate post-tax performance fees
revenue_streams.notes: A$35.6m FY2026 vs A$46.6m FY2025 (-24%), contributed by 12 of 19 Affiliates; inherently lumpy and market/style dependent

revenue_streams.name: Non-cash step-acquisition/fair-value gains on affiliate stake increases
revenue_streams.notes: A$52.3m non-cash gain in FY26 from PAM 25%->100%; not part of underlying earnings

business_model.customer_type: Indirect B2B2C — Affiliates serve institutional investors, superannuation funds, wholesale/financial adviser channels and increasingly Australian and international retail investors; Pinnacle's own direct customers are its Affiliates and the funds they manage
business_model.geographic_mix: FUM by source: Australian institutional and retail ~67%, international (UK, US, Canada, Asia, NZ, Europe) ~33% at FY2026, up from 2% at FY2016; Affiliates and staff based in Australia, UK, US, Canada, Japan and elsewhere

main_competitors: Global boutique aggregators (e.g. Affiliated Managers Group in the US)
competitive_position.market_position: Leading and largest ASX-listed multi-affiliate/multi-boutique asset management platform in Australia; effectively the category creator locally (founder Ian Macoun previously built Australia's first multi-boutique model at Perennial). No single ASX-listed peer replicates the full multi-affiliate structure at Pinnacle's scale (A$229.4bn FUM).

moat_factors.description: Centralised distribution, responsible-entity and operational infrastructure lets small boutiques access institutional, wholesale and retail channels (including offshore) they could not economically build alone; growing international distribution team (19-42 people including PAM) compounds this advantage as more Affiliates are added

Affiliates keep majority/founder equity, brand and investment autonomy while Pinnacle provides capital and infrastructure — reduces key-person departure risk relative to a fully-owned single-brand manager, and is attractive to boutique founders vs alternatives (acquisition by a bank, or staying independent without scale)

19 affiliates spanning equities, fixed income, private credit, private equity, infrastructure and real assets smooths earnings across market cycles and style rotations; performance fees came from 12 different affiliates in FY26 despite dispersion in individual style performance

Balance sheet capacity (including a A$250m CBA facility, fully drawn) to seed new strategies and fund equity stakes gives Pinnacle an edge in sourcing and closing new affiliate deals versus smaller aggregators
81% of group strategies with a 5-year record have beaten benchmark, consistently 80-90% over 10 years — a differentiator when pitching new mandates and new affiliate partnerships

weaknesses: Pinnacle does not own 100% of most Affiliates — profit share (e.g. ~37% affiliate profit share vs ~40% FUM share flagged by UBS on FY26 results) can lag FUM growth, and minority stakes limit capital allocation control

Affiliate expense growth can outpace revenue growth in strong years (FY26 affiliate expenses came in ~22% above consensus, partly performance-fee-linked staff incentives), compressing consolidated margins
Not immune to industry fee compression facing active managers generally; scale in distribution does not eliminate fee pressure at the underlying strategy level
Complexity of equity-accounting/consolidation transitions (e.g. PAM moving from equity method to full consolidation mid-FY26) makes period-on-period comparability difficult for investors
Concentration: a small number of large affiliates (Metrics, Hyperion, Antipodes, Coolabase, Firetrail) likely account for a disproportionate share of group profit

growth_drivers: New affiliate acquisitions/stake increases: Advantage Partners (Japan private markets, initial 5% Jan-2026, option to add 8% more), Pacific Asset Management (25%->100% April 2026), VSS Capital Partners (US structured capital, Nov-2024), and PAM's own bolt-on acquisition of Asset Value Investors (AVI, announced Aug-2026, ~£1.9bn FUM)

International distribution expansion — international distribution headcount growing (19 standalone, 42 including PAM); international-sourced FUM up from 2% (FY16) to 33% (FY26) of total, still well below domestic share, implying long runway

'Three Horizons' strategy: Horizon 1 (support existing affiliates), Horizon 2 (new affiliates/strategies, can dilute near-term margins), Horizon 3 (larger platform partnerships/international expansion, e.g. PAM)

Diversification into higher-growth/higher-fee asset classes: private markets (private equity, private credit, infrastructure) growing faster (38% 10-yr CAGR) than public markets (25%), and alternative fixed income (Coolabah) and private credit (Metrics, which itself acquired BC Invest and Taurus in July 2025 to expand consumer lending origination)
Performance fee optionality — FUM eligible for performance fees has grown from A$3.3bn (FY16) to A$61.3bn (FY26), a 34% CAGR, providing a growing (if volatile) base for outsized profit contribution

Retail channel build-out — retail FUM growth of 35% CAGR (vs 28% total), and multiple Affiliates listing retail-accessible vehicles on ASX (Plato's PL8/PGA1/PGI2 ETFs, Firetrail's ASX:FIRE, Solaris's ASX:SET IPO, Antipodes SMID ETF) broadening the addressable retail investor base
AI investment — Pinnacle is building dedicated capability for AI development/integration across the platform and Affiliates, a potential future efficiency/product driver

business.description: A relatively small number of larger, longer-tenured Affiliates (e.g. Metrics, Hyperion, Antipodes) likely drive a disproportionate share of group profit; underperformance or outflows at any one could meaningfully affect consolidated results

Boutique investment performance is often tied to a small number of named portfolio managers/founders; departure (e.g. departing Metrics executive Graham McNamara's family trust selling down its stake in 2026) can disrupt an Affiliate's franchise even though Pinnacle itself has limited control

Share of post-tax performance fees swung from A$46.6m (FY25, boosted by an exceptional Hyperion contribution) to A$35.6m (FY26, -24%); management explicitly warns predicting short-term performance fee outcomes is difficult

Moving Affiliates from equity-accounted to fully consolidated (PAM in FY26) adds cost, integration risk and short-term margin dilution; PAM's own bolt-on of AVI adds a further layer of integration risk one step removed from Pinnacle
Broader active-management industry faces continued fee compression from passive/ETF competition, which could pressure Affiliate revenue margins over time despite Pinnacle's distribution advantages

financial.description: CBA debt facility increased from A$100m to A$250m in FY26 and was fully drawn at year-end, partly funding Principal Investments and stake acquisitions; interest cost rose to A$7.9m (FY26) from A$6.5m (FY25)

Group holds A$196.5m in financial assets at fair value (mostly seed capital in Affiliate strategies); FY26 saw a net loss of A$2.3m on a mark-to-market basis and a net loss of A$7.5m after financing costs (vs a A$20.2m net gain in FY25) — a directly market-linked, volatile P&L line
Growing international Affiliates (PAM/AVI in GBP, VSS in USD, Advantage in JPY, Langdon in CAD) introduce multi-currency translation and economic exposure not previously significant

Large acquisitions have been funded via equity raises (A$441.8m capital raise disclosed for FY2025; ~A$400m institutional placement in Nov-2024 for VSS/PAM stakes) and scrip issuance (2,027,928 new shares for the AVI deal), diluting existing shareholders periodically

regulatory.description: Group operates in a highly regulated environment across multiple jurisdictions (AFSL/responsible entity obligations in Australia, plus UK, US, Japan, Canada regulatory regimes as international Affiliates and PAM/AVI scale up); management cites continual investment in Risk and Compliance to keep pace
Management specifically flagged that rapid growth of private credit in Australia (relevant to Affiliate Metrics) has prompted further regulatory/market scrutiny and caution

macro.risk: Equity market and investor sentiment sensitivity
macro.description: Management explicitly identifies investment market conditions as a major business risk; FUM, fee revenue and (especially) performance fees are directly linked to market levels and volatility, tariffs, geopolitical conflict and monetary policy shifts cited as FY26 sources of caution
Affects both fixed-income/credit Affiliate performance (Coolabah, Metrics) and the cost of Pinnacle's own drawn debt facility
Net inflows were record in FY26 (A$33.4bn) but management notes flows and earnings 'can moderate during times of market dislocation'; private equity exit conditions cited as currently challenging

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global and Australian active asset management faces structural fee pressure from passive investing, but private markets (private credit, private equity, infrastructure) continue to see strong structural demand from institutional and increasingly retail/wealth channels; multi-boutique aggregation is viewed as a resilient structural response to industry scale pressures
macro_factors.cyclicality: High — FUM, base fees and especially performance fees are directly linked to public and private market valuations and investor risk appetite; net flows and Principal Investments mark-to-market returns are pro-cyclical
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate — affects fixed income/credit affiliate strategies' relative attractiveness and cost of Pinnacle's own drawn debt; also affects valuations underpinning private markets affiliates
key_input_costs: Staff compensation/incentives (STI/LTI, which scale with performance and performance fees)

recent_developments.event: FY2026 full-year results: reported NPAT $176.7m (+31.5%), underlying NPAT (ex PAM step-acquisition gain and PI losses) $138m (+21%), diluted EPS 78.1cps (statutory) / 61cps underlying, final dividend 31.0cps (65% franked) taking FY26 total to 60.0cps; FUM $229.4bn (+28%), record net inflows $33.4bn

Analyst reaction mixed/'messy': FUM and net flows beat expectations but statutory profit missed consensus (UBS: ~25% miss on H2 driver; Jarden: EPS ~12% below consensus, ~7% ex non-operating items) due to affiliate expenses running ~22% above consensus (performance-fee-linked staff incentive pass-throughs) and affiliate profit share (~37%) trailing FUM share (~40%)

Pacific Asset Management (100%-owned since April 2026) agreed to acquire UK boutique Asset Value Investors (AVI, ~£1.9bn/A$3.6bn FUM, AVI Global Trust and AVI Japan Opportunity Trust); Pinnacle to issue 2,027,928 new shares (~A$31.9m) as part consideration; AVI to retain its own brand and investment approach
Matthew Lamb (CEO of PAM since 2016) appointed Executive Director of Pinnacle's Board effective 5 August 2026, remaining London-based

Pinnacle agreed to acquire an additional ~6.8% stake in Metrics Credit Holdings for ~A$100.5m from the McNamara Family Trust (departing executive Graham McNamara), restoring Pinnacle's stake to ~35% (its original 2018 level); National Pension Service of Korea concurrently increasing its Metrics stake to 9.9%; deal structured 75% on completion / 25% deferred 12 months, expected to complete Q2-Q3 CY2026

Pinnacle completed acquisition of the remaining 75.1% of Pacific Asset Management (from 25% to 100%) for A$215.7m cash (per management commentary) / reported acquisition payment of A$228.8m; recognised non-cash step-acquisition gain of A$52.3m and A$6.1m one-off transaction costs; PAM revenues/expenses now consolidated (previously equity-accounted)

Pinnacle acquired an initial 5% stake in Advantage Partners (Japan's largest independent multi-strategy private markets platform, founded 1992), its first Japanese Affiliate, with an option to acquire a further 8% over three years; Advantage closed Japan Buyout Fund VIII heavily oversubscribed at ¥300bn (May 2026)
recent_developments.note: first affiliate investment in Japan, diversifying geography and asset class

recent_developments.event: Affiliate Metrics Credit Partners completed acquisitions of BC Invest and Taurus, expanding consumer lending origination capability
Affiliate Riparian Capital Partners secured a cornerstone commitment from Australian Super fund Brighter Super for its Riparian Agriculture and Food Transition Strategy (QRAFT)

items.notes: Consistent with prior years, Pinnacle does not provide formal quantitative revenue/EPS/margin guidance and explicitly states it does not forecast future levels of financial markets

Chair notes opening FY27 FUM is 28% ahead of the level at which Pinnacle entered FY26, PAM is now a full part of the global platform for the first year, and the platform is 'well positioned to support further expansion and growth across multiple channels and jurisdictions', while flagging global volatility may produce challenges
This is an external analyst (per FNArena roundup of broker notes) projection, not company-issued guidance; included for context only

items.target: Expected to be the single largest year-on-year profit driver in FY27 (per broker commentary)
items.notes: PAM contributed from completion (24 April 2026) only in FY26; FY27 will capture a full 12 months of consolidated PAM profit plus the AVI bolt-on

items.target: Continuation of high payout ratio (FY26: 60.0cps total, in line with FY25's 60.0cps)
items.notes: Franking level moved to 72% blended for FY26 (from 79% in FY25) as offshore/consolidated earnings (e.g. PAM) generate less Australian franking credit

guidance.management_commentary: Chair Alan Watson: 'We enter FY27, recognizing global volatility may produce challenges, and as we have said previously, we do not forecast future levels of financial markets. Nevertheless, against that background, there remain grounds for cautious optimism.' Management reiterated that Horizon 2/3 growth initiatives (new affiliates, international expansion) can moderate near-term profitability but are pursued for medium-term returns, and that performance fees — while a 'significant factor' in earnings — are inherently difficult to predict short-term.

bull_case: Proven, scalable multi-affiliate model with a 10-year FUM CAGR of 28% and NPAT CAGR of 37%, still expanding into new geographies (Japan via Advantage, UK/Europe via PAM+AVI) and asset classes (private credit, private equity, infrastructure) with a long runway given international FUM is still only 33% of the total

PAM's move to full ownership plus the AVI bolt-on gives Pinnacle a materially larger, higher-margin global distribution and origination platform; FY27 will be the first full year of consolidated PAM profit, which brokers flag as the single largest identifiable profit driver for the year

Diversified performance-fee base (12 of 19 Affiliates contributed in FY26) reduces reliance on any one strategy/style, while a growing perf-fee-eligible FUM base (34% 10-yr CAGR) provides optionality for outsized profit in strong markets

Structurally aligned 'supported independence' model retains founder/staff equity at Affiliates, reducing key-person departure risk relative to fully-owned single-brand competitors, and continues to attract high-quality boutique partners (Five V, Advantage, VSS, PAM/AVI)
High and consistently growing dividend (34% 10-yr CAGR in DPS) with a payout policy tied to underlying earnings, supported by a capital-light equity-accounting model once initial stakes are seeded
bear_case: FY26 results were described by analysts as 'messy': despite FUM and flow beats, statutory profit missed consensus by a wide margin as affiliate expenses (particularly performance-linked staff incentives) grew faster than affiliate revenue, and Pinnacle's affiliate profit share trailed its FUM share — raising questions about margin capture as the platform scales

Performance fees are volatile and unpredictable by management's own admission (down 24% YoY in FY26 versus up strongly in FY25); a sustained market downturn or performance-fee drought at key Affiliates (Hyperion, Metrics, etc.) would directly hit group NPAT

Heavy and recurring M&A/capital deployment (PAM, Advantage, VSS, Metrics stake increase, AVI) funded partly by large equity raises (~A$400-442m placements) and scrip issuance creates recurring dilution risk and integration execution risk, particularly as the platform becomes more international and operationally complex

Rising leverage — CBA facility increased to A$250m and fully drawn at FY26 year-end — plus a directly market-linked Principal Investments book (which posted a net loss in FY26) adds financial and market risk on top of the core affiliate-profit-share earnings stream

Key-person/succession risk sits largely outside Pinnacle's direct control at the Affiliate level (e.g. a departing Metrics executive selling down a family trust stake in 2026), and Pinnacle's minority stakes in most Affiliates limit its ability to intervene directly in an underperforming or destabilised boutique
